## Data loading

```{r DataLoading, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# Cargamos los datos incorporando las modificaciones para trabajar con él
# https://zenodo.org/records/15535434
# Cuidado con el nombre de los ríos, hay besòs y bessos.
Riverbank <- 
  read.csv(file = "PlasticPirates_Riverbank_data/Riverbank_data_v2.0.0.csv", header = TRUE, sep = ",", na.strings = c("na", "NA")) %>% 
  dplyr::mutate(SamplingDate = lubridate::ymd(SamplingDate)) %>% 
  dplyr::mutate(across(where(is.character), as.factor))
```

## Pre-proccessing

```{r RiversName, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# Loading the rivers' dictionary
Riverbank_dictionary <- read_excel("Riverbank_data_v2.1.xlsx", sheet = "Final vocabulary clean")

Riverbank <-
  Riverbank %>%
  # The dictionary has one row per river AND country (e.g. "donau" for Austria and Germany),
  # so joining only by river would duplicate those samplings
  left_join(Riverbank_dictionary, by = c("SamplingRiver", "CountryResponsible" = "Country"),
            relationship = "many-to-one") %>%
    #dplyr::select(SamplingRiver, Corrected_river_English, SamplingRiverSystem, River_basin, everything()) %>% 
    dplyr::mutate(River_basin = str_remove(River_basin, regex("\\s+Basin$", ignore_case = TRUE))) %>% 
  dplyr::mutate(SamplingRiver = coalesce(Corrected_river_English, SamplingRiver),
         SamplingRiverSystem = River_basin) %>% 
  dplyr::select(-c("No", "Corrected_river", "Corrected_river_English", "River_basin", "Count of SamplingRiver")) %>%
  # 2021 has a single (non-validated) sampling from one country, so it is excluded from the whole analysis
  dplyr::filter(SamplingYear != 2021)

```

### Sampling Effort Description

The sampling effort of each Group B survey is defined by the size of the riverbank area searched, recorded in two attributes:

* `RiversideWasteVariety_Results_LengthOfRiverbankSearchedM`: length of the riverbank searched (m).
* `RiversideWasteVariety_Results_WidthOfRiverbankSearchedM`: width of the riverbank searched (m).

According to the dataset documentation (`READme_info_riverbank_v2.0.0.txt`), *"Data for length and width of riverbank searched for group B could not always be verified by the experts"*. Therefore, before using them (e.g. to standardise litter counts per m²), we describe (i) the amount of missing values and (ii) their variability, looking for outliers.

**Note:** the CSV codes missing values both as `"na"` and as `"NA"`. Both are declared as missing in `DataLoading` (`na.strings = c("na", "NA")`), so length and width are read as numeric. Otherwise, the width attribute would be read as text because of the literal `"NA"` cells.

```{r SamplingEffortData, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# Sampling effort dataset with short column names
Sampling_effort_data <-
  Riverbank %>%
  dplyr::transmute(
    DatasetID,
    CountryResponsible = str_to_title(CountryResponsible),
    SamplingYear,
    SamplingRiver,
    # Same criteria as GroupB_data_validated (NA counts as FALSE)
    Attempted = coalesce(RiversideWasteVariety_AttemptedSampling == 1, FALSE),
    Validated = coalesce(RiversideWasteVariety_AttemptedSampling == 1 &
                           RiversideWasteVariety_Qualified == 1, FALSE),
    Length_m = RiversideWasteVariety_Results_LengthOfRiverbankSearchedM,
    Width_m  = RiversideWasteVariety_Results_WidthOfRiverbankSearchedM,
    Area_m2  = Length_m * Width_m
  )

# Validated subset (the one used in the Group B analyses)
Sampling_effort_validated <- Sampling_effort_data %>% dplyr::filter(Validated)
```

#### Missing values

For each attribute we count the missing values (`NA`), and for the combination of both we count the *complete cases* (rows with both length and width). The *Incomplete* columns show how many records, and what percentage of the total, would be removed if we kept only complete cases. This is shown for the whole dataset, for the attempted samplings and for the validated Group B samplings (the subset used in the analyses).

```{r SamplingEffortNA, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# Summary of missing values (n and %) for length, width and their combination
na_summary <- function(data, subset_name) {
  data %>%
    summarise(
      Subset                 = subset_name,
      N                      = n(),
      `NA Length (n)`        = sum(is.na(Length_m)),
      `NA Length (%)`        = round(100 * mean(is.na(Length_m)), 1),
      `NA Width (n)`         = sum(is.na(Width_m)),
      `NA Width (%)`         = round(100 * mean(is.na(Width_m)), 1),
      `NA Both (n)`          = sum(is.na(Length_m) & is.na(Width_m)),
      `Incomplete (n)`       = sum(is.na(Length_m) | is.na(Width_m)),
      `Incomplete (%)`       = round(100 * mean(is.na(Length_m) | is.na(Width_m)), 1),
      `Complete cases (n)`   = sum(!is.na(Length_m) & !is.na(Width_m)),
      `Complete cases (%)`   = round(100 * mean(!is.na(Length_m) & !is.na(Width_m)), 1)
    )
}

Sampling_effort_NA <-
  bind_rows(
    na_summary(Sampling_effort_data, "All records"),
    na_summary(dplyr::filter(Sampling_effort_data, Attempted), "Attempted sampling"),
    na_summary(Sampling_effort_validated, "Validated (Group B)")
  )

Sampling_effort_NA
```

In the validated Group B dataset, `r Sampling_effort_NA$"Incomplete (n)"[3]` out of `r Sampling_effort_NA$N[3]` samplings (`r Sampling_effort_NA$"Incomplete (%)"[3]`%) lack the length, the width or both. Keeping only complete cases would remove that share of the data.

Missing values per country (validated Group B samplings), to check whether they are concentrated in a few countries:

```{r SamplingEffortNACountry, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
Sampling_effort_validated %>%
  group_by(CountryResponsible) %>%
  summarise(
    N                    = n(),
    `NA Length (n)`      = sum(is.na(Length_m)),
    `NA Width (n)`       = sum(is.na(Width_m)),
    `Incomplete (n)`     = sum(is.na(Length_m) | is.na(Width_m)),
    `Incomplete (%)`     = round(100 * mean(is.na(Length_m) | is.na(Width_m)), 1),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(`Incomplete (%)`))
```

#### Variability and outliers

Descriptive statistics of the validated Group B samplings. Zero values are also counted, since a searched length or width of 0 m is not plausible.

Both attributes are strongly concentrated around a few "standard" values (most samplings searched about 50 m × 20 m) and have long right tails. Under these conditions Tukey's IQR rule is not useful: the width IQR is very narrow (15–20 m), so the rule flags around a quarter of the samplings as outliers, even on a log scale. Instead, we flag as **extreme values** those below the lower or above the upper percentile set in `pct_limits` (by default the 1st and 99th percentiles), plus all zero values. The limits can be changed to make the criterion more or less strict.

```{r SamplingEffortStats, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# Percentiles defining the extreme values (change them for a more/less strict criterion)
pct_limits <- c(0.01, 0.99)

Sampling_effort_stats <-
  Sampling_effort_validated %>%
  dplyr::select(Length_m, Width_m, Area_m2) %>%
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "Variable", values_to = "Value") %>%
  dplyr::mutate(Variable = factor(Variable, levels = c("Length_m", "Width_m", "Area_m2"))) %>%
  group_by(Variable) %>%
  summarise(
    n            = sum(!is.na(Value)),
    `NA`         = sum(is.na(Value)),
    Zeros        = sum(Value == 0, na.rm = TRUE),
    Min          = min(Value, na.rm = TRUE),
    P_low        = quantile(Value, pct_limits[1], na.rm = TRUE),
    Q1           = quantile(Value, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE),
    Median       = median(Value, na.rm = TRUE),
    Mean         = round(mean(Value, na.rm = TRUE), 1),
    Q3           = quantile(Value, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE),
    P_high       = quantile(Value, pct_limits[2], na.rm = TRUE),
    Max          = max(Value, na.rm = TRUE),
    `Extreme (n)` = sum(Value < P_low | Value > P_high | Value == 0, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

Sampling_effort_stats
```

Both attributes are strongly right-skewed (the mean is much higher than the median), so the histograms use a logarithmic x-axis. Zero values cannot be shown on a log scale and are excluded from the plots (they are counted in the table above). The solid line marks the median and the dashed lines the percentile limits. The scatter plot combines both attributes; the grey diagonal lines show constant searched areas (100, 1,000, 10,000 and 100,000 m²).

```{r SamplingEffortPlot, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.width=12, fig.height=9}
# Limits (percentiles) and medians for the figures
get_stat <- function(var, stat) {
  Sampling_effort_stats %>% dplyr::filter(Variable == var) %>% pull(all_of(stat))
}
lim_L <- c(get_stat("Length_m", "P_low"), get_stat("Length_m", "P_high"))
lim_W <- c(get_stat("Width_m",  "P_low"), get_stat("Width_m",  "P_high"))
med_L <- get_stat("Length_m", "Median")
med_W <- get_stat("Width_m",  "Median")

# Classify each sampling as extreme in length, width or both
Sampling_effort_validated <-
  Sampling_effort_validated %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    Extreme_L = Length_m < lim_L[1] | Length_m > lim_L[2] | Length_m == 0,
    Extreme_W = Width_m  < lim_W[1] | Width_m  > lim_W[2] | Width_m  == 0,
    # A missing value does not count as extreme; NA only when both are missing
    Extreme   = case_when(
      is.na(Extreme_L) & is.na(Extreme_W)                     ~ NA_character_,
      coalesce(Extreme_L, FALSE) & coalesce(Extreme_W, FALSE) ~ "Length & Width",
      coalesce(Extreme_L, FALSE)                              ~ "Length",
      coalesce(Extreme_W, FALSE)                              ~ "Width",
      TRUE                                                    ~ "None"
    ),
    Extreme = factor(Extreme, levels = c("None", "Length", "Width", "Length & Width"))
  )

Sampling_effort_plot_data <-
  Sampling_effort_validated %>%
  dplyr::filter(Length_m > 0, Width_m > 0) %>%
  arrange(Extreme)  # extreme values are drawn on top

# Length histogram
Hist_length <-
  Sampling_effort_validated %>%
  dplyr::filter(Length_m > 0) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = Length_m)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = "#4A90E2", colour = "black") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = med_L, linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = lim_L, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = label_comma()) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.05))) +
  labs(x = "Length of riverbank searched (m, log scale)", y = "Number of samplings") +
  theme_classic()

# Width histogram
Hist_width <-
  Sampling_effort_validated %>%
  dplyr::filter(Width_m > 0) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = Width_m)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = "#B8D4F0", colour = "black") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = med_W, linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = lim_W, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = label_comma()) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.05))) +
  labs(x = "Width of riverbank searched (m, log scale)", y = "Number of samplings") +
  theme_classic()

# Length vs width scatter plot, with constant-area lines (L * W = A  ->  W = A / L)
Scatter_LW <-
  ggplot(Sampling_effort_plot_data, aes(x = Length_m, y = Width_m)) +
  geom_abline(intercept = log10(c(1e2, 1e3, 1e4, 1e5)), slope = -1,
              colour = "grey70", linetype = "dotted") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = lim_L, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = lim_W, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_point(aes(fill = Extreme), shape = 21, size = 2.5, alpha = 0.8,
             position = position_jitter(width = 0.02, height = 0.02, seed = 123)) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = label_comma()) +
  scale_y_log10(labels = label_comma()) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("None" = "grey80", "Length" = "#4A90E2",
                               "Width" = "#E69F00", "Length & Width" = "#D55E00")) +
  labs(x = "Length of riverbank searched (m, log scale)",
       y = "Width of riverbank searched (m, log scale)",
       fill = "Extreme value") +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

# Combined figure: histograms on top, scatter plot below
Sampling_effort_area <-
  (Hist_length + Hist_width) / Scatter_LW +
  plot_layout(heights = c(1, 1.6)) +
  plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A")

print(Sampling_effort_area)

if (save_figures) ggsave(filename = "Sampling_effort_area.png", plot = Sampling_effort_area, path = paste(getwd(), "/OUTPUT/FIGURES", sep = ""), scale = 1.5, width = 20, height = 16, units = "cm", dpi = 300, limitsize = FALSE)
```

Distribution of length and width per country, to check whether outliers are specific to some countries (zero values excluded):

```{r SamplingEffortCountryPlot, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.width=12, fig.height=6}
Sampling_effort_country <-
  Sampling_effort_validated %>%
  dplyr::select(CountryResponsible, Length_m, Width_m) %>%
  pivot_longer(c(Length_m, Width_m), names_to = "Variable", values_to = "Value") %>%
  dplyr::filter(Value > 0) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(Variable = recode(Variable, Length_m = "Length (m)", Width_m = "Width (m)")) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = CountryResponsible, y = Value)) +

  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))

print(Sampling_effort_country)
```

List of the validated samplings with extreme values (outside the percentile limits, or zero) in length or width, ordered by searched area, for manual checking:

### Most common types and quantities of litter per region? (Group B: riverbanks; Group C: floating litter)

#### Group B: Riverside Waste

Statistics of the variable `RiversideWasteVariety_AttemptedSampling` to see how many samplings were performed.
```{r GroupB, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE, eval=TRUE}
Riverbank %>% 
  dplyr::select(RiversideWasteVariety_AttemptedSampling) %>% 
  table()
```

To work with the `RiversideWasteVariety_` data, we need to filter the dataset to include only those rows where `RiversideWasteVariety_AttemptedSampling` is 1 (indicating that a sampling was attempted) and `RiversideWasteVariety_Qualified` is also 1 (indicating that the sampling was qualified).

```{r GroupBData, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE, eval=FALSE}
Riverbank %>% 
  dplyr::filter(RiversideWasteVariety_AttemptedSampling == 1 & RiversideWasteVariety_Qualified == 1)
```

##### Percentage of qualified samplings

This represents the percentage of validated data among the total number of sampling beign attempted.
```{r}
Riverbank %>%
  summarise(
    total_rows = n(),
    total_valid = sum(
      RiversideWasteVariety_AttemptedSampling == 1 &
      RiversideWasteVariety_Qualified == 1,
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),
    pct_valid_total = round((total_valid / total_rows) * 100, digits = 1),
    pct_valid_percent = paste(round((total_valid / total_rows) * 100, 1), "%", sep = "")
  )
```

```{r}
validated_pct_by_country <- 
  Riverbank %>% 
  group_by(CountryResponsible) %>% 
  summarise(total_rows = n(),
            total_valid = sum(RiversideWasteVariety_AttemptedSampling == 1 & RiversideWasteVariety_Qualified == 1, na.rm = TRUE),
    `pct_valid_total(%)`        = round((total_valid / total_rows) * 100,1),
    total_attempts         = sum(RiversideWasteVariety_AttemptedSampling == 1, na.rm = TRUE),
    valid_among_attempts   = sum(RiversideWasteVariety_AttemptedSampling == 1 & RiversideWasteVariety_Qualified == 1, na.rm = TRUE),
    `pct_valid_among_attempts(%)` = round((valid_among_attempts / total_attempts) * 100,1), .groups = "drop") %>% 
  dplyr::mutate(CountryResponsible = str_to_title(CountryResponsible))
```

Firstly, we will pick up data to answer the question about group B. Only some variables are taken from the general dataset.

```{r, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
# GroupB dataset
GroupB_data <- 
  Riverbank %>% 
  dplyr::select(DatasetID, CountryResponsible, SamplingCampaign, SamplingYear, SamplingCoordinatesLatitude, SamplingCoordinatesLongitude, SamplingRiverSystem, SamplingParticipants, RiversideWasteVariety_AttemptedSampling, RiversideWasteVariety_Qualified:RiversideWasteVariety_Results_ResultsComment)

```

The, Attributes' names are so complicated to work that I'll remote the preceding information **RiversideWasteVariety_Results_** which is common to all attributes; and finally to work with only the validated `Group B` dataset we create:

```{r, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
# GroupB dataset
GroupB_data_validated <- 
  Riverbank %>% 
  dplyr::select(DatasetID, CountryResponsible, SamplingCampaign, SamplingYear, SamplingCoordinatesLatitude, SamplingCoordinatesLongitude, SamplingRiverSystem, SamplingParticipants, RiversideWasteVariety_AttemptedSampling, RiversideWasteVariety_Qualified:RiversideWasteVariety_Results_ResultsComment) %>% 
  dplyr::filter(RiversideWasteVariety_AttemptedSampling == 1 & RiversideWasteVariety_Qualified == 1) %>% 
  # Primero quitamos `RiversideWasteVariety_Results_`
  rename_with(
    .cols = starts_with("RiversideWasteVariety_Results_"),
    # solo seleccionamos los tipos de residuos
    .fn = ~ gsub("RiversideWasteVariety_Results_", "", .) # Mantenemos la ultima extensión del nombre
  )

#GroupB_data_validated

GroupB_data_validated <-
  GroupB_data_validated %>% 
  dplyr::select(!SingleUsePlasticTotal)
```

###### Manuscript values: mean ± s.e. and n (Fig. 3 and Fig. 4)

Mean ± standard error (rounded to one decimal) and number of validated samplings (*n*) for the litter categories and countries cited in the Results section.

```{r ManuscriptLitterMeanSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# Mean ± s.e. and n per litter category, optionally grouped by other variables (e.g. country)
litter_mean_se <- function(data, cols, ...) {
  data %>%
    dplyr::mutate(CountryResponsible = str_to_title(CountryResponsible)) %>%
    pivot_longer({{ cols }}, names_to = "Litter_type", values_to = "Abundance") %>%
    group_by(..., Litter_type) %>%
    summarise(n    = n(),
              Mean = mean(Abundance),
              SE   = sd(Abundance) / sqrt(n()),
              .groups = "drop") %>%
    dplyr::mutate(Manuscript = sprintf("%.1f ± %.1f, n = %d", Mean, SE, n))
}

# Whole validated dataset (Fig. 3)
Litter_overall_mean_se <-
  litter_mean_se(GroupB_data_validated, PlasticBags:LocalWaste) %>%
  arrange(desc(Mean))

  litter_mean_se(GroupB_data_validated, PlasticBags:LocalWaste, CountryResponsible)

)

Litter_cited_pairs %>%
```

###### Litter type Proportion I - "Across‑type" proportions

* The first approach will be a "*Across‑type*" proportions. 
  * For each litter type, what fraction comes from each country? (not from an european total)
  * total abundance of that litter type over each total country.


```{r ProportionLitterCountry, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
Prop_Liter_Country <- 
  GroupB_data_validated %>%
  # 1) pivot to long form
  pivot_longer(
    cols      = PlasticBags:LocalWaste,
    names_to  = "Litter_type",
    values_to = "Abundance"
  ) %>%
  # 2) sum abundance by (Country, Type)
  group_by(CountryResponsible, Litter_type) %>%
  summarise(
    Total_Abundance = sum(Abundance, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  # 3) compute, per type, the global total
  group_by(Litter_type) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    Global_Total   = sum(Total_Abundance),
    Prop_Country   = Total_Abundance / Global_Total
  ) %>%
  ungroup()

Prop_Liter_Country
```

```{r ProportionLitterCountryPlot, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
  geom_col(position = "fill") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_format()) +
```

* Now, considering the total of Europe

```{r ProportionLitterEurope, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
# 1) Pivot, sum by country & type, then compute each country’s share of the European total
Data_prop_eu <- 
  GroupB_data_validated %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols      = PlasticBags:LocalWaste,
    names_to  = "Litter_type",
    values_to = "Abundance"
  ) %>%
  group_by(CountryResponsible, Litter_type) %>%
  summarise(
    Total_Abundance = sum(Abundance, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  group_by(Litter_type) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    European_Total   = sum(Total_Abundance),
    Prop_of_Europe   = Total_Abundance / European_Total
  ) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  # optional: title‑case and reorder types by overall Prop for consistent ordering
  dplyr::mutate(
    CountryResponsible = str_to_title(CountryResponsible),
    Litter_type        = reorder(Litter_type, -Prop_of_Europe)
  )

Data_prop_eu
```

Bootstrap implementation in the dendrograms nodes. It replaces the previous heatmap with the dendrograms based on bootstrap values.

```{r}
#library(pvclust)

# 1. Preparar la matriz de datos en formato wide (países como columnas)
mat <- Data_prop_eu %>%
  pivot_wider(id_cols = Litter_type,
              names_from = CountryResponsible,
              values_from = Prop_of_Europe) %>%
  column_to_rownames("Litter_type") %>%
  as.matrix()

# 2. Calcular el clustering con bootstrap (nboot = 1000 recomendado para publicación)
set.seed(123)  # reproducible bootstrap (AU/BP values)
pv_result <- pvclust(mat, method.hclust = "ward.D2",
                     method.dist = "euclidean", nboot = 1000)

# 3. Extraer el dendrograma con los valores AU
dend_with_bootstrap <- as.dendrogram(pv_result)

# 4. Pasar el dendrograma personalizado a tidyHeatmap
ProportionLitterEuropeHeatMap_pvclust <-
  Data_prop_eu %>%
  heatmap(
    .row           = Litter_type,
    .column        = CountryResponsible,
    .value         = Prop_of_Europe,
    scale          = "column",
    cluster_rows   = FALSE,
    cluster_columns = dend_with_bootstrap,   # <- dendrograma con bootstrap
    row_names_side = "left",
    row_title_side = "left",
    palette_value  = c("#F7FBFF", "#6BAED6", "#08306B"),
    name           = "Relative \nimportance (%)",
    column_title   = "Country",
    row_title      = "Litter type",
    show_row_names    = TRUE,
    show_column_names = TRUE
  )

ProportionLitterEuropeHeatMap_pvclust
```

```{r, include=FALSE}
# Save the plot

  png(filename = "OUTPUT/FIGURES/Proportion_Litter_Europe_HeatMap_pvclust.png", width = 25, height = 20, units = "cm", res = 300, pointsize = 1)
  print(ProportionLitterEuropeHeatMap_pvclust)
  dev.off()
}
```

Dendrogram with the values

```{r}
# Dendrograma con valores AU (rojo) y BP (verde) en cada nodo
plot(pv_result, main = "", sub = "", xlab = "")  # no titles in the paper; was: default pvclust title, subtitle and x label
pvrect(pv_result, alpha = 0.95)  # recuadra los clusters con AU >= 95%

# Save the plot
if (save_figures) {
  png(filename = "OUTPUT/FIGURES/Proportion_Litter_Europe_Clustering_Percentage.png", width = 25, height = 20, units = "cm", res = 300, pointsize = 10)
  plot(pv_result, main = "", sub = "", xlab = "")  # no titles in the paper; was: default pvclust title, subtitle and x label
  pvrect(pv_result, alpha = 0.95)
  dev.off()
}
```

```{r ProportionLitterCountryII, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
    values_to = "Abundance"
  ) %>%
  # 2) sum by (Country, Type)
  group_by(CountryResponsible, Litter_type) %>%
  summarise(
    Total_Abundance = sum(Abundance, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  # 3) compute, per country, that country’s total
  group_by(CountryResponsible) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    Country_Total = sum(Total_Abundance),
    Prop_Type     = Total_Abundance / Country_Total
  ) %>%
  ungroup()

Prop_Liter_Country2
```

###### Multivariate Perspective

```{r DataPreparationMultivariate}
# assume your data is in a data.frame called `df`
# and has at least:
#   CountryResponsible | PlasticBags | PlasticBottles | ... | LocalWaste
# Replace the NA values for 0. --> Probably the default behaviour?
df <- GroupB_data_validated %>% 
  dplyr::select(DatasetID, CountryResponsible, PlasticBags:LocalWaste) %>% 
  drop_na()
# mutate_all(funs(replace_na(.,0)))

# Filas sin ningún residuo (no se pueden transformar con Hellinger)
empty <- rowSums(dplyr::select(df, PlasticBags:LocalWaste)) == 0
# df %>% dplyr::filter(empty)   # para documentar qué muestreos se excluyen

df <- df %>% dplyr::filter(!empty)

# isolate metadata + community matrix
meta <- df %>% dplyr::select(DatasetID, CountryResponsible)
comm <- df %>% dplyr::select(PlasticBags:LocalWaste)

# Hellinger‐transform community data (recommended for PCA/cluster/PERMANOVA)
comm_hel <- decostand(comm, method = "hellinger", na.rm = TRUE)
```


In order to see if there are significant differences across country in the community composition, we will perform a PERMANOVA test:

```{r PermanovaTest, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# 2a) Compute distance and hierarchical clustering (Ward’s D2)
dist_mat <- vegdist(comm_hel, method = "euclid", na.rm = TRUE)

# 3a) PERMANOVA: test if composition differs by Country
set.seed(42)

perm1 <- adonis2(dist_mat ~ CountryResponsible, data = meta, 
                 permutations = 999, by = "margin", na.action = na.omit)
print(perm1)
```

So, we conclude that there are significant differences among countries.

We can look for **heterocedasticity** among countries (homogeneity of multivariate dispersions), since PERMANOVA can also detect differences in dispersion and not only in location:

```{r betadisperOverall, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
Overall_Disper <- betadisper(dist_mat, meta$CountryResponsible)

Overall_Disper

set.seed(42)  # reproducible permutation test
Overall_Disper_test <- permutest(Overall_Disper, permutations = 999)

Overall_Disper_test
```

The multivariate dispersion `r if (Overall_Disper_test$tab[1, "Pr(>F)"] < 0.05) "**differs significantly**" else "**does not differ significantly**"` among countries (betadisper; F = `r round(Overall_Disper_test$tab[1, "F"], 2)`, p = `r Overall_Disper_test$tab[1, "Pr(>F)"]`)`r if (Overall_Disper_test$tab[1, "Pr(>F)"] < 0.05) ", so part of the PERMANOVA result may reflect differences in within-country variability rather than only in composition" else ""`.

But what are the items that explain these differences? 

The answer will be addressed by performing a **Multivariate Random Forest**.

```{r MultRandFor, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# 3b) Multivariate Random Forest:  
#     predict Country from composition → variable importance
set.seed(42)  # reproducible random forest
rf <- randomForest(
  x      = comm_hel,
  y      = as.factor(meta$CountryResponsible),
  ntree  = 500,
  importance = TRUE
)

print(rf)
```

```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, echo=FALSE}
# Random Forest Evaluation
# El Mean Decrease Gini mide cuánto contribuye cada variable a la pureza de los nodos
importance_df <- as.data.frame(importance(rf))
importance_df$Variable <- rownames(importance_df)

# Accuracy
cm <- rf$confusion
accuracy <- sum(diag(cm[,-ncol(cm)])) / sum(cm[,-ncol(cm)])
```

Decisions have to be taken carefully since the prediction accuracy is very low (`r round(accuracy, 2)`). Furthermore, the estimated error rate (OOB) is high, so conclusion have to be taken with care. 

Eventhough, the more important (differential across countries) litter components are:

```{r RFVarImport, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, out.width="80%"}
varImpPlot(rf, main = "", type = 2)  # no titles in the paper; was: "Random Forest: Litter‐type Importance for Country Discrimination"
```

```{r, include=FALSE}
# Save the plot
if (save_figures) {
  png(filename = "OUTPUT/FIGURES/Random_Forest_Importance.png", width = 20, height = 16, units = "cm", pointsize = 10, bg = "white", res = 150)
  varImpPlot(rf, main = "", , type = 2)  # no titles in the paper; was: "Random Forest: Litter‐type Importance for Country Discrimination"
  dev.off()
}
```

This plot of variable importance importance is telling us:

<!--
*  A large `MeanDecreaseAccuracy` (**MDA**) means that, when you break the relationship between that predictor and the response, the model’s accuracy suffers a lot → it’s an important predictor for correct country assignments. 
  * **MDA** is generally the more reliable gauge of predictive importance, since it directly measures impact on OOB‐accuracy.
-->

* A large `MeanDecreaseGini` (**MDG**) means that X frequently appears in high‑up the tree splits and yields big purity gains → it’s structurally important to partitioning the data. 
  * **MDG** tells you which features the trees “prefer” splitting on.

* **Non-Metric Multidimensional Scaling - nMDS**

We will perform a Non-Metric Multidimensional Scaling (nMDS) to see correlation among litter items and *possible* associations with countries.

We can re-use the distance matrix using the hellinger‐transformed data (`comm_hel`) and then perform the nMDS.

```{r, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
# En la matriz de comm hay columnas con todo 0 (vacías) que pueden causar problemas en el análisis multivariante, así que las eliminamos antes de hacer el nMDS.
# Filas con todo 0 (vacías)
empty_rows <- which(rowSums(comm, na.rm = TRUE) == 0)

length(empty_rows)   # para ver cuántas hay
empty_rows           # opcional: ver índices concretos

# Eliminar esas filas de comm y de meta a la vez
if (length(empty_rows) > 0) {
  comm1 <- comm[-empty_rows, , drop = FALSE]
  meta1 <- meta[-empty_rows, , drop = FALSE]
} else {
  # comm ya viene sin filas vacías (filtradas en DataPreparationMultivariate)
  comm1 <- comm
  meta1 <- meta
}

# Repetimos la transformación Hellinger sobre la nueva matriz de comunidad sin filas vacías.
comm_hel1 <- decostand(comm1, method = "hellinger") #esto ya estaba definido.

set.seed(123)  # reproducibilidad

nmds <- metaMDS(
  comm_hel1,                 # matriz de comunidad (Hellinger‐transformed)
  distance      = "bray",  # típico en comunidad
  k             = 2,       # nº de dimensiones
  autotransform = FALSE    # ya transformaste con Hellinger
)

```

Now, we calculate the scores for the sites (samples) and add the metadata to be able to visualize the nMDS with the country information.
```{r, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
# scores de sitios
site_scores <- as.data.frame(scores(nmds, display = "sites"))  # NMDS1, NMDS2, ...

site_scores <- site_scores %>% 
  mutate(
    SampleID = rownames(.)
  )

# añadimos CountryResponsible alineando por fila
site_scores <- site_scores %>% 
  bind_cols(meta1)  # meta está en el mismo orden que comm/site_scores
```

```{r, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
ggplot(site_scores, aes(x = NMDS1, y = NMDS2, colour = CountryResponsible)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, alpha = 0.8) +
  theme_minimal() +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(x = "NMDS1", y = "NMDS2")
```

To see which countries are more similar than others, we can calculate the centroids of each country in the NMDS space and then plot them.

```{r, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
# centroides (medias) por país en el espacio NMDS
country_centroids <- site_scores %>% 
  group_by(CountryResponsible) %>% 
  summarise(
    NMDS1 = mean(NMDS1, na.rm = TRUE),
    NMDS2 = mean(NMDS2, na.rm = TRUE),
    n     = dplyr::n()
  )

ggplot() +
  geom_point(data = site_scores,
             aes(x = NMDS1, y = NMDS2, colour = CountryResponsible),
             alpha = 0.3, size = 2) +
  geom_point(data = country_centroids,
             aes(x = NMDS1, y = NMDS2, fill = CountryResponsible),
             size = 5, shape = 21, colour = "black") +
  ggrepel::geom_text_repel(
    data = country_centroids,
    aes(x = NMDS1, y = NMDS2, label = CountryResponsible),
    size = 3
  ) +
  coord_equal() +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(x = "NMDS1", y = "NMDS2")
```

From the above plot, we can say that the non-metric multidimensional scaling ordination based on Bray–Curtis dissimilarities of Hellinger-transformed litter composition revealed a clear gradient along the first two NMDS axes. Countries are arranged in a roughly linear sequence in this ordination space, indicating systematic shifts in the relative contribution of the different litter categories rather than discrete clusters. This pattern suggests that national litter profiles form a continuum, with some countries showing more similar compositions and therefore grouping closer together, while others occupy more distant positions along the gradient. Taken together, the NMDS indicates that between-country variation in litter is primarily structured along one dominant compositional axis, with a secondary axis capturing finer differences among otherwise similar profiles.

```{r ProportionLitterCountrySUP, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
SUP_Prop_Liter_Country <- 
  GroupB_SingleUsePlastic_data_validated %>% 
  dplyr::select(CountryResponsible, PlasticBags:Polystyrene) %>%  
  pivot_longer(
    PlasticBags:Polystyrene,
    names_to  = "Litter_type",
    values_to = "Abundance"

  summarise(
    Total_Abundance = sum(Abundance, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
```

###### SUP Multivariate Perspective

```{r DataPreparationMultivariateSUP}
# assume your data is in a data.frame called `df`
# and has at least:
#   CountryResponsible | PlasticBags | PlasticBottles | ... | LocalWaste

df_SUP <- GroupB_SingleUsePlastic_data_validated %>% 
  dplyr::select(CountryResponsible, PlasticBags:Polystyrene)
# %>% 
# #drop_na()
# mutate_all(funs(replace_na(.,0)))

# Filas sin ningún residuo SUP (no se pueden transformar con Hellinger: dan NaN)
empty_SUP <- rowSums(dplyr::select(df_SUP, -CountryResponsible)) == 0
df_SUP <- df_SUP %>% dplyr::filter(!empty_SUP)

# isolate metadata + community matrix
meta_SUP <- df_SUP %>% dplyr::select(CountryResponsible)
comm_SUP <- df_SUP %>% dplyr::select(-CountryResponsible)

# Hellinger‐transform community data (recommended for PCA/cluster/PERMANOVA)
comm_hel_SUP <- decostand(comm_SUP, method = "hellinger")

```


In order to see if there are significant differences across country in the community composition, we will perform a PERMANOVA test:

```{r PermanovaTest_SUP, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# 2a) Compute distance and hierarchical clustering (Ward’s D2)
dist_mat_SUP <- vegdist(comm_hel_SUP, method = "euclid")

# 3a) PERMANOVA: test if composition differs by Country
set.seed(42)

perm1_SUP <- adonis2(dist_mat_SUP ~ CountryResponsible, data = meta_SUP, 
                 permutations = 999, by = "margin")
print(perm1_SUP)
```

So, we conclude that there are significant differences among countries. The R-Square value (`r round(perm1_SUP$R2[1], 3)`) means that the country "effects" explain `r round(100 * perm1_SUP$R2[1], 1)`% of the total variability. `r round(100 * (1 - perm1_SUP$R2[1]), 1)`% is the remaining (unexplained) variability among countries. ***There is a significant country effect, but is small***.

Or even better:
**There are statistically significant multivariate differences in litter composition among countries, although the effect size is modest (R² = `r round(perm1_SUP$R2[1], 3)`).**

We can look for **heterocedasticity** among countries

```{r betadisper}
SUP_Disper <- betadisper(dist_mat_SUP, meta_SUP$CountryResponsible)

SUP_Disper
```

```{r betadisperSUPtest}
set.seed(42)  # reproducible permutation test
SUP_Disper_test <- permutest(SUP_Disper, permutations = 999)

SUP_Disper_test
```

The multivariate dispersion `r if (SUP_Disper_test$tab[1, "Pr(>F)"] < 0.05) "**differs significantly**" else "**does not differ significantly**"` among countries (betadisper; F = `r round(SUP_Disper_test$tab[1, "F"], 2)`, p = `r SUP_Disper_test$tab[1, "Pr(>F)"]`)`r if (SUP_Disper_test$tab[1, "Pr(>F)"] < 0.05) ", so we must be careful when concluding about the inter-country differences" else ", so the PERMANOVA result reflects differences in composition rather than in within-country variability"`. There is a Country effect but it is small.

If we need to parametrize this model, we should use a Mixed Multivariate Model (necessary?)

```{r mvabund, echo=FALSE, eval=FALSE}
# modelo lineal multivariado generalizado (PERMANOVA Multivariado)
library(mvabund)

mv_data <- mvabund(comm_matrix)

fit <- manyglm(mv_data ~ CountryResponsible,
               family = "negative.binomial")

anova(fit, p.uni = "adjusted")

# Modelo mixto jerárquico bayesiano

brm(
  mvbind(PlasticBags, PlasticBottles, ...) ~ 1 + (1|CountryResponsible),
  family = negbinomial(),
  data = data
)
```


but What are the items that explains these differences? 

The answer will be addressed by performing a **Multivariate Random Forest**.

```{r MultRandForSUP, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# 3b) Multivariate Random Forest:  
#     predict Country from composition → variable importance
set.seed(42)  # reproducible random forest
rf_SUP <- randomForest(
  x      = comm_hel_SUP,
  y      = as.factor(meta_SUP$CountryResponsible),
  ntree  = 500,
  importance = TRUE
)

print(rf_SUP)
```
```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, echo=FALSE}
# Random Forest Evaluation
# El Mean Decrease Gini mide cuánto contribuye cada variable a la pureza de los nodos
Sup_importance_df <- as.data.frame(importance(rf_SUP))
Sup_importance_df$Variable <- rownames(Sup_importance_df)

# Accuracy
Sup_cm <- rf_SUP$confusion
Sup_accuracy <- sum(diag(Sup_cm[,-ncol(Sup_cm)])) / sum(Sup_cm[,-ncol(Sup_cm)])
```

Decisions have to be taken carefully since the prediction accuracy is very low (`r round(Sup_accuracy, 2)`). Furthermore, the estimated error rate (OOB) is high, so conclusion have to be taken with care. 

Even though, the more important (differential across countries) litter components are:

```{r RFVarImportSUP, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
varImpPlot(rf_SUP, main = "", type = 2)  # no titles in the paper; was: "Random Forest: 'Sigle Use Plastic-type' Importance for Country Discrimination"
```

```{r, include=FALSE}
# Save the plot
if (save_figures) {
  png(filename = "OUTPUT/FIGURES/Random_Forest_Importance_SUP.png", width = 22, height = 12, units = "cm", pointsize = 10, bg = "white", res = 150)
  varImpPlot(rf_SUP, main = "", type = 2)  # no titles in the paper; was: "Random Forest: 'Sigle Use Plastic-type' Importance for Country Discrimination"
  dev.off()
}
```

This plot of variable importance importance is telling us:

*  A large `MeanDecreaseAccuracy` (**MDA**) means that, when you break the relationship between that predictor and the response, the model’s accuracy suffers a lot → it’s an important predictor for correct country assignments. 
  * **MDA** is generally the more reliable gauge of predictive importance, since it directly measures impact on OOB‐accuracy.

* A large `MeanDecreaseGini` (**MDG**) means that X frequently appears in high‑up the tree splits and yields big purity gains → it’s structurally important to partitioning the data. 
  * **MDG** is faster to compute and tells you which features the trees “prefer” splitting on, but can overweight high–cardinality or continuous variables.
  
Finally, we will perform a Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to see correlation among litter items and *possible* associations with countries

```{r PCASUP, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
# ─── 1) PCA (and optional RDA constrained by Country) ───────────────────────────
# 1a) Unconstrained PCA on Hellinger data

# 
# summary(pca1)
# 
# plot(pca1)

pca_prcomp_SUP <- prcomp(comm_hel_SUP, scale. = TRUE)

#summary(pca_prcomp_SUP)
```

###### Manuscript values: Table 2 (PERMANOVA)

PERMANOVA results for the overall litter dataset (`perm1`) and the SUP subset (`perm1_SUP`), in the layout of Table 2 of the manuscript.

```{r ManuscriptTable2, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# Tidy adonis2 output (one row per term)
tidy_permanova <- function(perm, analysis) {
  as.data.frame(perm) %>%
    rownames_to_column("Term") %>%
    dplyr::transmute(
      Analysis = analysis,
      Term     = recode(Term, CountryResponsible = "Country", Residual = "Residuals"),
      df       = Df,
      SS       = round(SumOfSqs, 3),
      F        = round(F, 2),
      R2       = round(R2, 3),
      p_value  = `Pr(>F)`
    )
}

Table2_PERMANOVA <-
  bind_rows(tidy_permanova(perm1,     "Overall analysis"),
            tidy_permanova(perm1_SUP, "Single-Use Plastics (SUP)"))

Table2_PERMANOVA

# Homogeneity of multivariate dispersions (betadisper) reported in the Results text
tibble(
  Analysis = c("Overall analysis", "Single-Use Plastics (SUP)"),
  F        = round(c(Overall_Disper_test$tab[1, "F"], SUP_Disper_test$tab[1, "F"]), 2),
  p_value  = c(Overall_Disper_test$tab[1, "Pr(>F)"], SUP_Disper_test$tab[1, "Pr(>F)"])
)
```


#### Macrolitter Flow calculation

The variable `FlowMacrolitter` is represented as the Number of floating macrolitter $m^{-1}$ $h^{-1}$.

```{r flowCalculation, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
FlowData <- 
  Floating_data %>% 
  dplyr::mutate(
    TimeInHours = as.numeric(FloatingMacro_ObservationTimeInMinutes/60),
    RiverWidth = as.numeric(FloatingMacro_ObservedWidth),
    FlowMacrolitter = as.numeric(FloatingMacro_AmountOfFloatingMacrolitter) /(RiverWidth * TimeInHours))

FlowData  
```

#### Macrolitter Flow Visualization

##### Differences across countries

Notes on the figures:

* **All sampling years are always shown** for every country. Country-year combinations without valid data are labelled **n.d.** (no data). This covers both years without floating samplings and years where the flow could not be calculated (e.g. the river width is missing).
* The number above each box is the number of valid samplings (*n*).
* Most flow values are exactly 0, so the y-axis uses a **square-root scale**. This spreads out the small values near zero while keeping the zeros, which a log scale cannot show. All observations are drawn as points over the boxes.
* No observations are removed from the plot. The previous version used `scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1))`, which **dropped** the values above 1 before computing the boxplots.

```{r FlowPlotData, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# Sampling years and colours (same palette as the rest of the document)
flow_years  <- sort(unique(FlowData$SamplingYear))
year_colors <- c("2021" = "#E0FFFF", "2022" = "#B8D4F0", "2023" = "#4A90E2", "2024" = "#1E3A8A")

# Valid observations only (flow could be calculated)
Flow_plot_data <-
  FlowData %>%
  dplyr::filter(!is.na(FlowMacrolitter)) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(SamplingYear = factor(SamplingYear, levels = flow_years))

# Number of samplings and valid values for every country-year combination,
# including those without any sampling (n = 0)
Flow_n <-
  FlowData %>%
  dplyr::mutate(SamplingYear = factor(SamplingYear, levels = flow_years)) %>%
  group_by(CountryResponsible, SamplingYear) %>%
  summarise(n_samplings = n(),
            n_valid     = sum(!is.na(FlowMacrolitter)),
            .groups = "drop") %>%
  complete(CountryResponsible, SamplingYear,
           fill = list(n_samplings = 0L, n_valid = 0L)) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(label = if_else(n_valid == 0, "n.d.", as.character(n_valid)))

# Common y-axis (square-root scale, keeps the zeros)
flow_y_scale <-
  scale_y_sqrt(breaks = c(0, 0.05, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 6),
               expand = expansion(mult = c(0.02, 0.12)))

Flow_n
```

* Boxplots per country, with the sampling years nested within each country on the x-axis:

```{r FloatingMacrolitterCountries, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.width=12, fig.height=6}
Floating_Macrolitter_Countries <-
  ggplot(Flow_plot_data, aes(x = SamplingYear, y = FlowMacrolitter, fill = SamplingYear)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA, width = 0.7) +
  geom_point(position = position_jitter(width = 0.15, height = 0, seed = 123),
             size = 0.8, alpha = 0.4) +
  # n (valid samplings) above each box, or "n.d." when there are no data
  geom_text(data = Flow_n,
            aes(x = SamplingYear, y = Inf, label = label,
                fontface = if_else(n_valid == 0, "italic", "plain")),
            inherit.aes = FALSE, vjust = 1.5, size = 2.6) +
  # One panel per country; years nested below, country names under the years
  facet_grid(. ~ CountryResponsible, switch = "x") +
  scale_x_discrete(drop = FALSE) +
  flow_y_scale +
  scale_fill_manual(values = year_colors, drop = FALSE) +
  labs(x = NULL,
       y = expression(Floating~macrolitter~(m^{-1}~h^{-1})~"(square-root scale)"),
       fill = "Sampling Year") +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(strip.placement  = "outside",
        strip.background = element_blank(),
        strip.text       = element_text(face = "bold", size = 9),
        panel.spacing.x  = unit(0.15, "lines"),
        panel.border     = element_rect(colour = "grey80", fill = NA),
        axis.text.x      = element_text(angle = 90, vjust = 0.5, hjust = 1, size = 8),
        legend.position  = "none")

Floating_Macrolitter_Countries
```

###### Manuscript values: low floating macrolitter densities

Summary of floating macrolitter flow (items m⁻¹ h⁻¹) per country, pooling all years, to fill the sentence on the countries with low densities (Belgium, Greece, Hungary and Latvia).

```{r ManuscriptFloatingLow, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
Flow_country_summary <-
  Flow_plot_data %>%
  group_by(CountryResponsible) %>%
  summarise(n      = n(),
            Median = median(FlowMacrolitter),
            Mean   = mean(FlowMacrolitter),
            SE     = sd(FlowMacrolitter) / sqrt(n()),
            Q75    = quantile(FlowMacrolitter, 0.75),
            Max    = max(FlowMacrolitter),
            .groups = "drop") %>%
  dplyr::mutate(across(Median:Max, ~ round(.x, 3)))

Flow_country_summary

# Countries cited as having low densities, per year (medians and maxima)
Flow_plot_data %>%
  dplyr::filter(CountryResponsible %in% c("Belgium", "Greece", "Hungary", "Latvia")) %>%
  group_by(CountryResponsible, SamplingYear) %>%
  summarise(n = n(), Median = round(median(FlowMacrolitter), 3),
            Max = round(max(FlowMacrolitter), 3), .groups = "drop")
```

* **Statistical test**

  * Generalize linear mixed model (Tweedie)

  Family error distribution was selected due to the data restriction (only positive values with high numbers of zeroes)

 
```{r}
Float_Macro_model <- glmmTMB(
  FlowMacrolitter ~ CountryResponsible,
  family = tweedie(link = "log"),
  data = FlowData
)

summary(Float_Macro_model)
```
 
```{r}
# Cálculo del valor de País

# Modelo completo (con CountryResponsible)
mod_full <- glmmTMB(FlowMacrolitter ~ CountryResponsible, family = tweedie(link = "log"), data = FlowData)

# Modelo nulo (sin CountryResponsible)
mod_null <- glmmTMB(FlowMacrolitter ~ 1, family = tweedie(link = "log"), data = FlowData)

anova(mod_null, mod_full)
```


* Posthoc with multple comparisons

```{r}
emmeans_mod <- emmeans(Float_Macro_model, pairwise ~ CountryResponsible, type = "response")

# Resultados de comparaciones ajustadas
summary(emmeans_mod$contrasts, adjust = "tukey")
```
